JUSTICE S.G.PANDIT AND HON'BLE DR. JUSTICE PRADEEP SINGH YERUR WA No. 2476 of 2015 C/W 101 OTHERS CAV JUDGMENT (PER: HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE S.G.PANDIT) The above batch of appeals and writ petitions arise out of common facts and as they involve common questions of law, they are heard together and disposed of by this common judgment. W.A.No.2476/2015 and connected appeals arise out of learned Single Judge's order dated

2015 in W.P.No.21216/2014 and connected writ petitions whereby writ petitions are allowed, striking down the Karnataka Private Aided Educational Institutions Employees (Regulation of Pay, Pension and Other Benefits) Act, 2014 (for short, 'Act No. 7 of 2014'), holding that the Act No.7 of 2014 is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India and encroaches upon the jurisdictional powers of the Courts, with a further direction to the State to continue to pay salary or pension as the case may be, as was being paid pursuant to its earlier orders or in other C/W 101 OTHERS words h1as been paid prior to impugned enactment, with other consequential directions. In W.A.No.100003/2021 and other connected appeals, the challenge is to order dated 24.07.2020 in W.P.No.105439/2014 and W.P.No.108382-417/2014, whereby the learned Single Judge allowed the writ petitions, quashed the impugned Act No.4 of 2015 i.e., the Karnataka Education Amendment Act, 2014 (for short, 'Act No. 4 of 2015'), amendment to Section 87 of Karnataka Education Act, 1983 (for short, 'Act, 1983') with a further direction to the State to consider the cases of the petitioners to grant additional increment for passing Kannada Language Examination, in accordance with law. For the sake of convenience, the parties hereinafter are referred to as they stood before the learned Single Judge. The appellants-State Authorities are referred to as C/W 101 OTHERS Respondents and respondents herein are referred to as petitioners. Brief facts of the case are that, as stated above, W.A.No.2476/2015 arises out of order dated

2015 in W.P.No.21216/2014 and connected matters. In W.P.No.21216/2014, the challenge was to Act No.7 of 2014, whereunder, Section 3 would state that, notwithstanding anything contained in State Of Karnataka vs Chandrashekar on 24 July, 2026 the Karnataka Education Act, 1983, any order of Government or Rules governing service conditions of employees of any Educational Institution or any other Law Governing grant-in-aid to the above employees or any judgment, decree or order of any Court or Tribunal or Authority, the grant-in-aid admissible to a post held by an employee of private aided educational institution shall be fixed and calculated at the minimum of pay scale admissible to that post from the date of admission to grant. Further, it would also state that the service rendered prior to admission for grant-in-aid shall not be reckoned for the purpose of pay, C/W 101 OTHERS leave, seniority and pension, and further, finalization of pensionary benefits shall be by non-reckoning the service rendered in non-grant period as qualifying years. It was the case of the petitioners that they were initially appointed to teaching or non-teaching posts in private aided institutions by the Management and subsequent to their appointment, the post in which they were working was admitted to grant-in-aid and thereafter they requested to count their services prior to admission to grant i.e., from the date of their initial appointment for the purpose of financial benefits i.e., for the purpose of pay fixation, pension and pensionary benefits. The petitioners pleaded that this Court on several earlier occasions had held that the employees of private aided institutions are entitled to count their past services prior to grant-in-aid for the purpose of pay fixation, pension and pensionary benefits on par with the government teachers. Those orders were taken up to the Hon'ble Apex Court and the State's Special Leave Petitions came to be dismissed. Learned Single Judge C/W 101 OTHERS taking note of the earlier orders, struck down the Act No. 7 of 2014, holding that there was no defect or lacuna in the enactment to render the judgments already delivered by the Courts to be ineffective, with further observations that on the ground of financial burden, the State Administration cannot shirk its responsibility of ensuring proper education in schools and colleges.

In W.A.No.100003/2021, the order under challenge is dated 24.07.2020 in W.P.No.105439/2014 and connected matters, wherein, the petitioners had challenged the Act No.4 of 2015, by which, the State amended proviso to section 87 of the 1983 Act. Prior to the amendment Section 87 read as follows: "87. Qualification, Conditions and Service of employees:- The state government may after previous publication make rules regulating the recruitment and conditions of service (including rights as regards disciplinary matters) of the employees in recognized private educational institutions. C/W 101 OTHERS Providing that the minimum qualification for recruitment, age of recruitment, and retirement and benefits of retirement for employees in educational institutions receiving maintenance grant from the state government shall be the same as those applicable for the corresponding category of employees, if any, in the state institutions unless otherwise prescribed."

By Act No.4 of 2015, in the first proviso "and benefits of retirement" were omitted and second and third proviso were inserted to deny one additional increment on passing of the Kannada Language Examination in terms of the Karnataka Civil Services (Services and Kannada Language Examination) Rules, 1974 (for short, 'Rules, 1974'). Subsequent to amendment, Section 87 reads as follows: State Of Karnataka vs Chandrashekar on 24 July, 2026 "87. Qualifications, conditions of service of employees. --The State Government may after previous publication make rules regulating the recruitment and conditions of service (including rights as regards disciplinary matters) of the employees in recognised private educational institutions: Provided that the minimum qualifications for recruitment, age of recruitment, and retirement for C/W 101 OTHERS employees in educational institutions receiving maintenance grant from the State Government shall be the same as those applicable for the corresponding category of employees, if any, in State Institutions unless otherwise prescribed. Provided further that conditions of service of the employees working in aided educational institutions shall be as such as may be determined by the State Government from time to time. Provided also that since 1974 no employee of the aided institution is required to appear and pass any Service Examination or the Kannada Language Examination as prescribed in the Karnataka Civil Service (Service and Kannada Language Examination) Rules, 1974 and no such employee shall be eligible for or be granted any additional increment for having passed or deemed to have been passed said examination from the date of commencement of said rules."

By virtue of Act No.4 of 2015, the State Government denied the employees of the aided private educational institutions, one additional increment for having passed Kannada Language Examination. The petitioners therein were teaching and non-teaching staff of the private C/W 101 OTHERS educational institutions contending that several orders of this Court passed prior to the amendment directed and held that the employees of private aided educational institutions would also be entitled to one additional increment for passing Kannada Language Examination. Learned Single Judge on consideration of the entire material on record, held that the Act No.4 of 2015 is an attempt by the State Legislature to escape the financial liability and the same is liable to be struck down on the ground of irrationality and arbitrariness and also violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India. Questioning both the orders of the learned Single Judge, the above appeals are preferred under Section 4 of the Karnataka High Court Act, 1961 by the State of Karnataka.

State Of Karnataka vs Chandrashekar on 24 July, 2026 Learned Additional Advocate Generals appearing on behalf of the State contended that learned Single Judge in both the orders under appeal committed a grave error in declaring Act No.7 of 2014 as well as Act No.4 of 2015 as unconstitutional without appreciating the fact that it was within the legislative power of the State to enact. It is C/W 101 OTHERS submitted that though the legislature has no competence or power to directly overrule the judgment or orders of this Court, it possesses the power to remove the basis or to remove the defect or mistake in its previous legislation, so as to render the judgments delivered by this Court to be ineffective.

Learned Additional Advocate Generals would submit that prior to coming into force of Act, 1983, the employees of the private aided institutions were governed by the triple benefit scheme insofar as pension and pensionary benefits are concerned and insofar as other service conditions, they were governed by the Karnataka Private Educational Institutions (Discipline) Act, 1975 (for short, 'Act, 1975') along with control of appointment under the grant-in-aid quota. Further, it is submitted that under Rule 52 of Triple benefit scheme, the service, either temporary, officiating or permanent rendered in State aided institution only shall be counted for the purpose of length of qualifying service. C/W 101 OTHERS Referring to various orders passed by the learned Single Judge as well as Co-ordinate Division Bench of this Court, it is submitted that though there was no provision for counting past service i.e., prior to admission to grant-in-aid for the purpose of pay fixation, pension and pensionary benefits, it was directed to count non-grant period for the purpose of pay, pension and pensionary benefits. Therefore, to remove the legal basis on which earlier judgments were rendered, the present enactments i.e., Act No.7 of 2014 as well as Act No.4 of 2015 were necessitated. Learned Additional Advocate Generals placing reliance on the decision of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of VIRENDER SINGH HOODA V. STATE OF HARYANA1 and GOA FOUNDATION V. STATE OF GOA2 contended that it is within the legislative power of the State to remove the legal basis and to render the judgments ineffective. (2004) 12 SCC 588 (2016) 6 SCC 602 C/W 101 OTHERS

On behalf of the State, it is contended that no Rule or provision is pointed out by the petitioners enabling them to claim or to count past service rendered prior to admission to grant for the purpose of pay, pension and pensionary benefits. When there is no provision or Rule to count the non-grant period, it is submitted that the Courts could not have directed counting of non-grant period for the purpose of pay, pension and pensionary benefits. Further, learned Additional Advocate Generals would contend that the State has no role in the appointment of staff of the private aided educational institutions and it is the sole prerogative of the management of the private aided educational institution to appoint their staff. It is submitted that the State would get control over the staff only after they are admitted to grant. Therefore, it is contended that the service rendered prior to grant cannot be counted for any other purpose and only service rendered subsequent to grant shall be counted for all financial benefits. Learned Additional Advocate Generals referring to section 87 C/W 101 OTHERS of 1983 Act would submit that the service conditions of the employees of private aided State Of Karnataka vs Chandrashekar on 24 July, 2026 institutions and government servants shall be the same, unless otherwise prescribed. As there is no Rule permitting to count the non-grant period for the purpose of pay, pension and pensionary benefits, it is contended that the petitioners would not be entitled for counting the non-grant period for any financial benefits.

Further, learned Additional Advocate Generals would contend that the power to enact a law also includes with it the power to give retrospective effect to the law. For the said contention, reliance is placed on the decisions of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of B.K. PAVITHRA V. UNION OF INDIA3 and STATE BANK'S STAFF UNION (MADRAS CIRCLE) V. It is also contended that a person would be entitled to be admitted to grant depending on the financial capability of the State and grant-in-aid to the post would depend on whether such employee fulfils the qualification roster and whether while appointing him, prescribed procedure is followed. It is also contended that the grant-in-aid cannot be claimed as a matter of right and it would depend on the criteria prescribed under grant-in-aid code. Further, it is contended that the employees of Private Aided Institutions cannot be granted benefit or benefits more than what the Government Teachers would be entitled to. It is contended that, from the date of admitting a particular post to grant-in- aid, all benefits available to a government teacher is extended to a teacher who is admitted to grant. Moreover it is contended that petitioners have failed to point out any C/W 101 OTHERS particular instance of discrimination. Learned Additional Advocate Generals would contend that the Hon'ble Apex Court has made it clear that the Courts while dealing with the matter involving financial implications shall be slow in interfering or the Courts shall consider such cases, keeping in mind the financial capability and constraints of the State. Thus, they would seek to allow the writ appeals by setting aside the orders of both the learned Single Judges. Per contra, learned counsels appearing for the petitioners would contend that Act No.7 of 2014 denying reckoning of service rendered prior to grant-in-aid for all financial benefits and Act No.4 of 2015 denying one additional increment for having passed Kannada language examination, was introduced only to over-rule the earlier judgments or C/W 101 OTHERS orders of learned Single Judge as well as the Co-ordinate bench of this Court. Further, it is contended that by virtue of subsequent legislation, the State could not nullify the earlier judgments or orders of the Court, that too, after giving an undertaking before the Court to comply with judgments or orders in Contempt proceedings. Further, learned counsels would submit that the Legislature has power to legislate to remove any defect or mistake in its earlier legislation or the legal basis in a judgment or order. However, they submit that such legislation cannot be enacted for the sole purpose of nullifying a judgment or order. In the instant case, it is contended that the Acts under challenge nullified earlier State Of Karnataka vs Chandrashekar on 24 July, 2026 judgments or orders of this Court which had become final on dismissal of SLPs filed by the State before the Hon'ble Apex Court.

Learned counsels for the petitioners i.e., respondents herein referring to Rule 52 of Triple Benefits Scheme would submit that it permits counting of service C/W 101 OTHERS rendered even as temporary, officiating or permanent employee in State Aided Institutions for all purposes. Further, they submit that the Institutions in which, the respondents were appointed were admitted to grant prior to their appointment and some of the posts were admitted to grant subsequent to the institution being admitted to grant. Therefore, it cannot be contended by the State that their services rendered prior to admitting their post to grant cannot be counted.

Learned counsels for the petitioners further referring to grant-in-aid Code of Primary and Secondary School Department would submit that every educational institution shall apply for permission and recognition to grant- in-aid Code and only the Educational Institution which is permitted and recognized by the State Government shall be entitled to seek grant-in-aid. Further, referring to Rule 16 of grant-in-aid Code, it is submitted that every recognized institution shall subject itself to the departmental inspection at C/W 101 OTHERS any time and shall abide by instructions issued by the Inspecting officer from time to time. It is submitted referring to Rule 17 of grant-in-aid Code that qualifications of all teachers shall be the same as those prescribed for similar category of Staff in Government Schools. Union of India, 1976 SCC OnLine Cal 108] of the Calcutta High Court was not a mere C/W 101 OTHERS declaratory judgment holding an impost or tax as invalid so that a validating statute can remove the defect pointed out in the judgment. He observed that the judgment [All India Insurance Employees' Assn. v. Union of India, 1976 SCC OnLine Cal 108] of the Calcutta High Court gave effect to the rights of the petitioners by mandamus, directing LIC to pay annual cash bonus. As long as the judgment [All India Insurance Employees' Assn. v. Union of India, 1976 SCC OnLine Cal 108] of the learned Single Judge is not reversed in appeal, it cannot be disregarded or ignored. The permissibility of legislative override in this country should be in accordance with the principles laid down by this Court in the aforementioned as well as other judgments, which have been culled out as under: The effect of the judgments of the Court can be nullified by a legislative act removing the basis of the judgment. Such law can be retrospective. Retrospective amendment should be C/W 101 OTHERS reasonable and not arbitrary and must not be violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution. [Lohia Machines Ltd. v. Union of India, (1985) 2 SCC 197 : 1985 SCC (Tax) 245] 50.2. The test for determining the validity of a validating legislation is that the judgment pointing out the defect would not have been passed, if the altered position as sought to be brought in by the validating statute existed before the Court at the time of State Of Karnataka vs Chandrashekar on 24 July, 2026 rendering its judgment. In other words, the defect pointed out should have been cured such that the basis of the judgment pointing out the defect is removed. Nullification of mandamus by an enactment would be impermissible legislative exercise (see : S.R. Bhagwat [S.R. Bhagwat v. State of Mysore, (1995) 6 SCC 16 : 1995 SCC (L&S) 1334] ). Even interim directions cannot be reversed by a legislative veto (see : Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal [Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal, In re, 1993 Supp (1) SCC 96 (2)] and Medical Council of India v. State of Kerala [Medical Council of India v. State of Kerala, (2019) 13 SCC 185] ). Transgression of constitutional limitations and intrusion into the judicial power C/W 101 OTHERS by the legislature is violative of the principle of separation of powers, the rule of law and of Article 14 of the Constitution of India.

The learned Attorney General asserted that this Court cannot direct the legislature to make law. He relied upon the judgment in Ashwani Kumar v. Union of India [Ashwani Kumar v. Union of India, (2020) 13 SCC 585] wherein it was held that it is beyond the competence of this Court to direct legislature to make law. There is no quarrel with the said proposition. The learned Attorney General further asserted that the direction given by this Court in MBA (3) [Madras Bar Assn. v. Union of India, (2021) 7 SCC 369] relating to the number of candidates to be recommended for appointment to each post can only be taken to be a suggestion. State of Bihar, (2006) 8 SCC 381 : 2006 SCC (L&S) 1986] that directions given under Article 142 are not law laid down by the Supreme Court under Article Any order not preceded by any reason or consideration of any principle is an order under Article

Karnail Singh [Union of India v. Karnail Singh, (1995) 2 SCC 728] , it makes the law operational to make it a binding precedent for the future instead of keeping it vague. In short, it declares the law, as under Article 141 of the Constitution. "Declaration of law" as contemplated in Article 141 of the Constitution is the speech express or necessarily implied by the highest Court of the land. The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within the territory of India under Article 141, whereas, Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to issue directions to do complete justice. Under Article 142, the Court can go to the extent of relaxing the application of law to the parties or exempting altogether the parties from the rigours of the law in view of the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case. [State of Punjab v. Rafiq Masih, (2014) 8 SCC 883 : (2014) 4 SCC (Civ) 657 : (2014) 6 SCC (Cri) 154 : (2014) 3 SCC (L&S) 134; State v. Kalyan Singh, (2017) 7 SCC 444 : (2017) 3 SCC (Cri) 408] Sufficient reasons were given in MBA (3) [Madras Bar Assn. v. The Hon'ble Apex Court has also held that retrospective legislation, though permissible, would be still amenable to judicial review under Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. A careful examination of the earlier judgments passed by this Court would clearly establish that the conclusions reached therein were not founded merely upon the wording of Section 87 of the Act, 1983 alone. The earlier judgments were rendered after an elaborate consideration of the entire statutory framework governing aided educational institutions, the nature of service rendered by employees of aided institutions, the parity to be maintained between employees of aided institutions and government institutions and the constitutional mandate of equality flowing under Article 14 of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, the orders/judgments of this Court were not only based on Section 87 of Act, 1983, but on examination of the relevant rules applicable to the employees of Aided Educational Institutions on the touchstone of Article 14 of the Constitution of India. When teaching and non-teaching staff of Aided Education Institutions perform identical duties, both during the non-grant period as well as during grant-in-aid period, the service rendered by them prior to grant cannot be ignored.

The principle of 'equal pay for equal work' and parity in service conditions formed the very foundation of the earlier judgments rendered by this Court. C/W 101 OTHERS

The employees continue to discharge the same teaching and non-teaching functions both during the non- grant period and after admission to grant. The institutions continue to remain recognised institutions governed by the statutory educational framework. The service rendered prior to grant continues to remain actual and uninterrupted service. The constitutional mandate to the State, as upheld by this Court in Unni Krishnan case [(1993) 1 SCC 645] -- to provide free education to the children up to the age of fourteen -- cannot be permitted to be circumvented on the ground of lack of economic capacity or financial incapacity. It is high time that the State must accept its responsibility to extend free education to the children up to the age of fourteen. Right to education is equally guaranteed to the children who are above the age of fourteen, but they cannot enforce the same unless the economic capacity and development of the State permits the enforcement of the same. The State must endeavour to review and increase the budget allocation under the head 'Education'. The Union of India must also consider to increase the percentage of allocation of C/W 101 OTHERS funds for "Education" out of the Gross National Product." What the impugned enactments, i.e., Act No.7 of 2014 and Act No.4 of 2015 seek to do is merely to declare that notwithstanding the earlier judgments, the service rendered during the non-grant period shall not be reckoned and the claims arising therefrom shall stand extinguished as well as non-grant of one increment for having passed the Kannada Language Examination. Such an exercise, in our opinion, does not amount to removal of the legal basis of the earlier judgments.

In the present case, no defect as such was ever pointed out in the earlier judgments requiring legislative curing. The earlier judgments did not strike down any statutory provision nor did they identify any lacunae in the legislation which required curing. On the contrary, the earlier judgments interpreted the existing statutory framework and C/W 101 OTHERS consistently held that employees of private aided institutions are entitled to parity in pensionary and service benefits. State Of Karnataka vs Chandrashekar on 24 July, 2026

The impugned enactments therefore do not cure any defect pointed out by the Court. Nor do they fundamentally alter the legal framework upon which the earlier judgments were rendered. The enactments merely seek to negate the effect of the earlier judgments and deprive the employees of the benefits recognised thereunder. Such an exercise amounts to legislative overruling simpliciter and not a valid exercise of removal of legal basis. Thus, having held that neither the legal basis is removed nor any defect is cured, the decision laid down in NHPC LTD. V. STATE OF H.P. reported in (2023) 17 SCC 1 becomes aptly applicable to the facts of the present case. The relevant portion is extracted hereunder: "35. What follows from the aforesaid judicial precedent is, a legislature cannot directly set aside a judicial decision. However, when a competent legislature retrospectively removes the substratum or foundation of a judgment to make the decision ineffective, the same is a valid legislative exercise provided it does not transgress C/W 101 OTHERS on any other constitutional limitation. Such a legislative device which removes the vice in the previous legislation which has been declared unconstitutional is not considered to be an encroachment on judicial power but an instance of abrogation recognised under the Constitution of India. The decisions referred to above, manifestly show that it is open to the legislature to alter the law retrospectively, provided the alteration is made in such a manner that it would no more be possible for the court to arrive at the same verdict. In other words, the very premise of the earlier judgment should be removed, thereby resulting in a fundamental change of the circumstances upon which it was founded.

The power of a legislature to legislate within its field, both prospectively and to a permissible extent, retrospectively, cannot be interfered with by courts provided it is in accordance with the Constitution. It would be permissible for the legislature to remove a defect in an earlier legislation, as pointed out by a constitutional court in exercise of its powers by way of judicial review. This defect can be removed both prospectively and retrospectively by a legislative process and previous actions can also be validated. However, where a legislature merely seeks to validate the acts carried out under a previous C/W 101 OTHERS legislation which has been struck down or rendered inoperative by a court, by a subsequent legislation without curing the defects in such legislation, the subsequent legislation would also be ultra vires. Such instances would amount to an attempt to "legislatively overrule" a court's judgment by a legislative fiat, and would therefore be illegal and a colourable legislation." (emphasis supplied)

Moreover, the decision of the Hon'ble Apex Court in S.R. BHAGWAT AND ORS. V. STATE OF MYSORE reported in (1995) 6 SCC 16 would also be applicable. It is now well settled by a catena of decisions of this Court that a binding judicial pronouncement between the parties cannot be made ineffective with the aid of any legislative power by enacting a provision which in substance overrules such judgment and is not in the realm of a legislative enactment which displaces the basis or foundation of the judgment and uniformly applies to a class of persons concerned with the entire subject sought to be covered by such an enactment having retrospective effect. We may only refer to two of these judgments. C/W 101 OTHERS

A Constitution Bench of this Court in the case of Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal, Re [1993 Supp (1) SCC 96 (2) : 1991 Supp (2) SCR 497] had to pronounce on the validity of Karnataka Cauvery Basin Irrigation Protection Ordinance, 1991 by which an interim order passed by a statutory tribunal supported by the decision of this Court dated 26-4- 1991 which had ruled that the Tribunal had power to consider the question of granting interim relief since it was specifically referred to it, was sought to be displaced. In paragraph 76 of the Report the following observations were made: (SCC p. 142) "The principle which emerges from these authorities is that the legislature can change the basis on which a decision is given by the Court and thus change the law in general, which will affect a class of persons and events at large. It cannot, however, set aside an individual decision inter partes and affect their rights and liabilities alone. Such an act on the part of the legislature amounts to exercising the judicial power of the State and to functioning as an appellate court or tribunal." In the case of G.C. Kanungo v. State of Orissa [(1995) 5 SCC 96 : JT (1995) 4 SC 589] a Division Bench of this Court speaking through Venkatachala, J., had to consider the validity of Arbitration (Orissa Second Amendment) Act, 1991 which sought to nullify the awards made by the Special Arbitration Tribunals constituted under the 1984 Amendment C/W 101 OTHERS Act, in exercise of the power conferred upon them by the Act itself. 114) "Thus, the impugned 1991 Amendment Act seeks to nullify the awards made by the Special Arbitration Tribunals constituted under the 1984 Amendment Act, in exercise of the power conferred upon them by that Act itself. (See Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal, Re [1993 Supp (1) SCC 96 (2) : 1991 Supp (2) SCR 497] .) From this, it follows that the State Legislature by enacting the 1991 Amendment Act has encroached upon the judicial power entrusted to judicial authority resulting in infringement of a basic feature of the State Of Karnataka vs Chandrashekar on 24 July, 2026 Constitution -- the Rule of Law.

Thus, when the 1991 Amendment Act nullifies the awards of the Special Arbitration Tribunals, made in exercise of the judicial power conferred upon them under the 1984 Amendment Act, by encroaching upon the judicial power of the State, we have no option but to declare it as unconstitutional having regard to the well-settled and undisputed legal position that a legislature has no legislative power to render ineffective the earlier judicial decisions by making a law which C/W 101 OTHERS simply declares the earlier judicial decisions as invalid and not binding, for such powers, if exercised, would not be legislative power exercised by it, but judicial power exercised by it encroaching upon the judicial power of the State vested in a judicial tribunal as the Special Arbitration Tribunal under the 1984 Amendment Act. C/W 101 OTHERS We may note at the very outset that in the present case the High Court had not struck down any legislation which was sought to be re-enacted after removing any defect retrospectively by the impugned provisions. Lastly, learned Additional Advocate Generals appearing on behalf of the State contended that the State would be put to great financial difficulties if the impugned Acts are struck down and any benefit that could be extended to employees of private aided educational institutions would depend on the financial capabilities of the State. When the teachers and other employees of private educational institutions discharge the same duties and responsibilities as that of similarly situated Government teachers and employees C/W 101 OTHERS of Government education department, they would be entitled to the same benefit which are extended to the teachers of Government educational institutions. On the ground of financial constraints or difficulty, persons discharging identical and similar duties cannot be treated unequally. Article 14 of the Constitution of India endeavors that the State shall not deny any person equality before law or equal protection of laws. A legislation which treats similarly situated persons unequally is liable to be struck down as violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India. A law being challenged as violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India has to pass the test of intelligible differentia as laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court in various decisions and one of them being STATE OF PUNJAB VS. The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of CHANDIGARH ADMINISTRATION VS. RAJNI VALI AND OTHERS (2000) 2 SCC 42 has held that, financial constraints or financial burden is not a reason for the State to shirk away from its responsibilities. Relevant extract of RAJNI VALI (supra) reads as under: "10. The aforesaid decision lays down that mere financial constraints or burden on the State exchequer cannot be a reason to deny a benefit to a similarly situated employee. A perusal of the Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to Act No. 7 of 2014 and Act No. 5 of 2015 would indicate that the predominant object behind the enactment of the impugned Acts was to avoid the substantial financial liability that would arise upon implementation of the orders/judgments rendered by this Court. However, once it has been held that the employees of private aided educational institutions are similarly situated to government employees, possessing the same qualifications and discharging identical duties, mere financial difficulties cannot amount to a constitutionally permissible basis for denying them parity in service benefits. Consequently, even assuming that the impugned enactments disclose an intelligible differentia, the object sought to be achieved, namely, reduction of financial burden on the State, C/W 101 OTHERS bears no rational nexus to the discriminatory classification introduced by the impugned enactments. The impugned Acts, therefore, fail to satisfy the second limb of the test i.e., the differentia having rational nexus with the objects sought to be achieved by the law and hence, are liable to be struck down on this ground as well.

Moreover, Section 49 of Act, 1983 requires State Government to set apart a sum of money annually for being given as grant-in-aid to local authority institutions and private institutions in the State within the economic capacity of the State. Section 49 (1) of Act, 1983 reads as follows: "49. Government to set apart sum for giving grant -in-aid to certain recognised institution.- (1) The State Government shall within the limits of its economic capacity, set apart a sum of money annually for being given as grant-in-aid (hereinafter in this Act referred to as grant) to local authority institutions and private institutions in the State recognised for this purpose in accordance with rules made in this behalf." Prior to amendment, Section 87 of Act, 1983 prescribed the minimum qualifications for recruitment, age of recruitment and retirement and benefits of retirement of C/W 101 OTHERS employees in private educational institutions similar to that of corresponding employees of State institutions. Section 49 of Act, 1983 requires State Government within its economic capacity to set apart grant-in-aid. Both the above Sections read harmoniously require the State to maintain the same standard of education in private educational institutions that of Government institutions. It is the bounden responsibility of the State to provide similar benefit in all respects that are available to State Government teachers to that of teachers of private educational institutions, that too, when the private educational institutions are discharging the duties and responsibilities of State in the matter of imparting education. It is also necessary to clarify the extent of the relief that would flow from the present judgment. The issue involved in the present batch of matters is confined to whether the service rendered by employees during the non-grant period is liable to be reckoned for the purpose of fixation of pay and other consequential service benefits. Neither the provisions C/W 101 OTHERS governing grant-in-aid nor the statutory framework casts any liability upon the State to pay salary for the period prior to admission of the post to grant-in-aid. As produced supra, Annexure-I of Rules, 1999 would make it abundantly clear that the management shall be liable for payment of salary and other benefits till the date such posts are admitted into grant- in-aid. The liability to pay salary during the non-grant period continues to rest upon the management of the concerned institution. Consequently, the service rendered during the said period shall be taken into account only for the purpose of notional fixation of pay as on the date of admission of the post to grant-in-aid and for extending consequential benefits such as pension and other service benefits. The employees shall not be entitled to claim arrears of salary or any other monetary benefits from the State for the period preceding the admission of the post to grant-in-aid.
